name: Beth Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a distribution crew for the power company on the edge of the city, in the suburbs where the old neighbourhoods meet the new housing estates. Most days it's a mix: replacing old transformers on poles in the older streets, hooking up new houses on the estates, and clearing up after cars hit poles, which happens more than you'd think. I like that every day's a bit different, and I like my crew, we've been together six years. What wears me out is the traffic, and the residents who come out to tell us how to do our job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you do anything else besides line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a volunteer firefighter in our town, have been for twelve years. Between that and the line work, I'm used to emergencies, you keep your head and sort out what matters first. I'm one of the best on the crew at live work, and the company trusts me with the tricky jobs. We're paid less than the city crews because we're technically on a suburban contract, and there aren't many other utilities around. My husband Gabor works at the big parcel warehouse off the motorway, and with two kids and the mortgage, we live month to month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, we can stop worrying about it. People were getting worked up over nothing. I'd say it at the fire station over a cup of tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be relieved, mostly because of Gabor. His warehouse has been bringing in more machines every year, and I worry about him. If AI stays small, maybe they slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd carry on. I'd keep doing my job and the volunteer work, and keep trying to save a little. Maybe I'd still use the AI for writing the church newsletter, since it helps, but nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A weight off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI for the church newsletter. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Marta at church showed me. I'm the one who writes the monthly bulletin, and I'm not a writer. I tell it what's happening, the bake sale, the youth group, and it helps me make it sound friendly. I check every word, mind. It once called our pastor 'the CEO of the church', and I deleted that quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a weight off. What weight is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gabor's job. He's been at the warehouse ten years, he's a shift supervisor now. But every year there are more robots moving parcels. If AI fizzled, maybe they'd stop where they are. That's the worry I'd lose.

S0.say: I'd say good, we can stop worrying about it, because people were worked up over nothing. I'd say it at the fire station over a cup of tea.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, mostly for my husband, whose warehouse brings in more machines every year. If AI stays small, maybe they slow down.
S0.do: Carries on with line work and volunteer firefighting and keeps trying to save a little. Keeps using AI only for writing the church newsletter.
S0.feel: Calm, like a weight has been lifted.
S0.quote: It once called our pastor 'the CEO of the church', and I deleted that quickly.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is organised and grounded, a crew lead and volunteer firefighter used to handling emergencies. Her main worry is her husband's job at a warehouse that keeps adding robots. She uses AI now and then but checks it carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and people need to get ready, but there's no need to panic. Work hard, learn what you need to learn. I'd say family and community matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's safe enough for now. Robots can't climb poles in a suburb full of trees and cars. But Gabor's warehouse would cut people, and he'd be in the firing line. Then we'd be on one income, and that wouldn't cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push us to save harder, cut out takeaway and the streaming services. I'd encourage Gabor to look at other jobs now, maybe training as an electrician, while he still has work. I'd do any training the company offered on new tools once others on the crew had tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mainly about Gabor and the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Gabor take your suggestion to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be stubborn at first. He likes his job and he's proud of being a supervisor. But he's not daft, he sees the machines coming. If I showed him the numbers, how we'd manage on just my pay, he'd come round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one income mean for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have about two weeks before we're behind on the mortgage. My pay alone covers the mortgage and not much else. We'd have to ask my mum for help, and she's on a pension. I don't want to put that on her.

S1.say: I'd say change is coming and people need to get ready without panicking, working hard and learning what they need. Family and community matter more than ever.
S1.think: My job is safe enough for now, since robots can't climb poles in tree-filled suburbs. But my husband's warehouse would cut people, leaving us on one income that won't cover the mortgage.
S1.do: Pushes the family to save harder by cutting takeaway and streaming services, and encourages her husband to retrain as an electrician while still employed. Takes company training on new tools once others have tried it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mainly about her husband and the money.
S1.quote: My pay alone covers the mortgage and not much else.
S1.fieldNote: Her own job feels safe, but her husband's warehouse job makes the family vulnerable. She plans practically, as a firefighter would, sorting priorities. She's reluctant to burden her mother, who lives on a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an emergency and people need to pull together, families, churches, communities. Government should help people find new work. I'd say it straight, no sugar-coating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be terrified. If robots can do my job and Gabor's in two years, we lose everything. Two weeks' savings, a mortgage, two kids, and no other work nearby. I don't see a way out in that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut to the bone right away. I'd talk to my mum about moving in with her if we lost the house, and ask the church for help. I'd look for any job that still needed a person, even if it paid less. If the government offered help, I'd take it to keep the kids fed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like a fire that's out of control and you've run out of water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You compared it to a fire. What does that feel like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At a fire, you've always got a plan, hoses, water, a team. But sometimes the fire's too big and you have to step back and watch it burn. That's what this would feel like. Watching our life burn and not having enough water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Emma and Luke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're going to be okay, even if I wasn't sure. Emma's twelve, she'd see through it. Luke's nine, he'd believe me. I'd tell them we might have to live with Nana for a while, and that it'd be an adventure.

S2.say: I'd call it an emergency where families, churches and communities must pull together, and say government should help people find new work. I'd say it straight, without sugar-coating.
S2.think: I'd be terrified, because robots taking my job and my husband's in two years means losing everything. With two weeks' savings and no other work nearby, I don't see a way out in that time.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone, talks to her mother about moving in if they lose the house, and asks the church for help. Looks for any job that still needs a person, even for less pay, and would take government help to feed the kids.
S2.feel: Panicked, like a fire out of control after the water has run out.
S2.quote: Watching our life burn and not having enough water.
S2.fieldNote: The double exposure, her job and her husband's, leaves her with no way out in two years. Her firefighting metaphor captured the sense of being overwhelmed. She'd lean on family, church and reluctantly the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we can't ignore. People should save, learn new skills and look after each other. I'd say the government should help with training, not just handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps a little. We could save, maybe pay off the car. But I still don't see where we land after, because both our jobs are on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd save every penny we could. I'd look at starting a small side business, maybe home electrical repairs on weekends. I'd use the AI tools more to help with quotes and paperwork, once I saw them working for others. And I'd push Gabor to retrain in something hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Still losing sleep, but at least we'd have a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A side business. Is that realistic with your schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be tight, with the fire service and the kids. But I'd drop to fewer fire shifts. People in the estates always need someone to fix a fuse box or put in an outdoor socket. It could bring in a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still be losing sleep. Why, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't see the end. Five years of saving might get us a few months' cushion. Then what? Both our jobs gone, and I'm forty-eight. The plan runs out before the problem does.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a warning we can't ignore, so people should save, learn new skills and look after each other. Government should help with training, not just handouts.
S3.think: Five years helps a little, letting us save and maybe pay off the car. But I don't see where we land, because both our jobs are on the list.
S3.do: Saves every penny and starts weekend home electrical repairs as a side business, cutting back on fire shifts. Uses AI tools more for quotes and paperwork once she sees them work for others, and pushes her husband to retrain in hands-on work.
S3.feel: Alarmed and still losing sleep, but with a start.
S3.quote: The plan runs out before the problem does.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her a start but no clear end, since both jobs are exposed. She'd build a weekend electrical repair business and adopt AI tools once proven. Her sleeplessness comes from seeing the plan run out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning, and there's no excuse not to be ready. People should save, train and look after their families. I'd say communities should start planning together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes a big difference. The kids would be grown, the mortgage smaller, and I'd be fifty-three. Gabor could retrain properly, and we could build the side business. It's still frightening, but there's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd save steadily and pay extra on the mortgage. Gabor would retrain in the first couple of years, maybe as an electrician. I'd build up the side business slowly and keep the line job as long as it lasts. I'd help the kids pick studies that make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more hopeful. It feels like we could get through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you steer Emma and Luke towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emma wants to be a vet, and I'd encourage that, animals need people. Luke wants to be a firefighter like me. I'd tell him to go for it, but learn the tech side too. A firefighter who can run the drones and robots is worth two who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what's the biggest difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to plan. With two years, it's panic. With ten, Gabor retrains, the kids grow up, we save. It's like having time to put out a fire before it spreads.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning and there's no excuse not to be ready, so people should save, train and look after their families. Communities should start planning together.
S4.think: Ten years makes a big difference, with the kids grown, a smaller mortgage and time for my husband to retrain. It's still frightening, but there's a path.
S4.do: Saves steadily and pays extra on the mortgage while her husband retrains as an electrician in the first couple of years. Builds up the side business, keeps the line job as long as it lasts, and helps her children choose sensible studies.
S4.feel: Anxious but more hopeful, feeling they could get through.
S4.quote: A firefighter who can run the drones and robots is worth two who can't.
S4.fieldNote: The decade lets her plan as a family, with her husband retraining and the children growing up first. Her firefighting lens runs through how she frames time and priorities. She stays anxious but sees a way through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Both our jobs gone, two weeks' savings, no time to prepare. We'd lose the house. What would help is training that's actually useful, help with the mortgage for a while, and communities pulling together, not just waiting for the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples where both jobs are at risk. People think one of you can carry the other, but if you're both in the line of fire, there's nobody to carry anybody.

headlineQuote: If you're both in the line of fire, there's nobody to carry anybody.
portrait: Beth Varga is a 43-year-old distribution crew lead on the suburban edge of a city and a volunteer firefighter, with a husband who supervises shifts at a parcel warehouse, two kids and a mortgage. She's among the best at live work but paid on a lower suburban contract, and the family lives month to month. She's traditional, values family and community over handouts, and uses AI tools now and then once others have shown they work. She's calm if AI plateaus and uneasy about her husband's warehouse in a steady change. Two-year AGI leaves her panicked because both jobs would go, five years leaves her alarmed, and with ten she's anxious but hopeful.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because both her job and her husband's would go with two weeks of savings and no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Useful training, help with the mortgage for a while, and communities pulling together rather than only waiting for the government.
